questions.q: Two developers compare --extendedDiagnostics output from their laptops before and after a change. Which lines can they compare directly?
questions.explain: Times and memory depend on the machine and its load. Counts only change when the code, the dependencies or the compiler change, so they are the reliable way to spot a regression.
options: Check time and Total time
Files, Types and Instantiations: they are the same on every machine for the same code and TypeScript version
Memory used
None of them

questions.q: What does the Instantiations line of --extendedDiagnostics count?
questions.explain: Generic, conditional, mapped and recursive types all produce instantiations. It is the best stable predictor of check time, which is usually the phase that grows out of control.
options: The number of classes created with new
How often a generic type was filled in with specific type arguments during checking
The number of files instantiated from templates
The number of import statements

questions.q: The catalogue has 301 source files, but --extendedDiagnostics reports 600 files. Where do the others come from?
questions.explain: Every declaration file the program reaches must be read and bound, even with skipLibCheck. Heavy dependencies add to parse time on every run.
options: Test files
TypeScript's lib files and the declaration files of dependencies reached through imports, such as @types/node and Zod
The dist folder
Duplicate counting

questions.q: With skipLibCheck: true, what does the compiler do with a dependency's .d.ts files?
questions.explain: Your code still gets the library's types. What is skipped is checking the declarations themselves, which is most of the extra work in the lesson's measurements.
options: It does not read them at all
It reads them and uses their types, but does not type-check their contents
It checks them only once per day
It replaces them with any

questions.q: What can go unnoticed with skipLibCheck: true?
questions.explain: It skips every declaration file, not only those in node_modules. Run a check with --skipLibCheck false now and then, and after changing declarations or upgrading type packages.
options: Type errors in your .ts source files
Errors inside your own hand-written .d.ts files, and conflicts between libraries' declarations
Missing modules
Syntax errors in .ts files

questions.q: Timings are noisy, so a measurement script takes the median of five runs. What does it print?
questions.explain: The median ignores the one slow run in each list (a busy moment on the machine), which the average would not. Even so, only compare times from the same machine, and prefer counts where you can.

questions.q: TypeScript 7 runs several checkers in parallel by default. Why can the Types count differ from a --singleThreaded run of the same project?
questions.explain: Parallel checking trades some duplicated work for shorter wall-clock time. In the lesson it took about two thirds of the single-threaded time.
options: Parallel checking skips some files
Each checker creates some types of its own for the files it handles, so the total differs; compare counts only between runs with the same settings
Single-threaded mode uses skipLibCheck
It is random

questions.q: How many paths does a settings type have when every level has 8 keys? What does this print?
questions.explain: Each level adds width ** level new paths. At depth 6 the union would pass the 100,000-member limit, even though the source only gained one level.

questions.q: Why does a recursive Paths<T> type get expensive so quickly?
questions.explain: Nothing in the source grows exponentially, but the type's output does. Measure it, and bound it with a depth limit.
options: Template literal types are always slow
The number of union members it must build multiplies by the number of keys at every extra level, so the work grows exponentially with depth
Recursion is not allowed in type aliases
Each path is checked at runtime

questions.explain: The lesson's five-digit order reference hit TS2590 at exactly 100,000 members. Even the "allowed" 10,000-member union is a heavy type to compare against; string formats with many values belong in runtime checks and branded types.

questions.q: What does TS2589, "Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite", mean?
questions.explain: In the lesson, Repeat<"-", 30> was fine and Repeat<"-", 60> hit the limit, because each level waited inside a template string for the next.
options: The program has an infinite loop
A recursive type had to be expanded more levels than the compiler allows; it cannot tell a very deep type from an endless one, so it stops
A file imports itself
The project has too many files

questions.q: What makes a recursive conditional type "tail recursive", and what does that buy?
questions.explain: Tail position removes the depth limit, not the work: 500 steps are still 500 steps wherever the type is used.
options: It recurses on the last type parameter; it makes the type cheaper
The recursive call is the entire result of its branch (partial results are carried in an extra parameter), so the compiler can loop instead of nesting, and allows far more iterations
It uses infer; it removes all limits and all cost
It is declared at the end of the file

questions.q: How does Paths<T, Depth extends unknown[] = []> with Depth["length"] extends 3 ? never : … limit the type?
questions.explain: A tuple's length is a literal number type, which makes it a counter the type system can compare. Paths deeper than the cap are simply not produced.
options: It checks the runtime length of the settings object
Each recursive step passes [...Depth, unknown], so the tuple's length counts the levels, and at three the type returns never instead of recursing
It limits the number of keys per level to three
It makes the union's members three characters long

questions.q: For the same four-level settings, Paths needed 17,362 instantiations with anonymous nested object types but 781 with named City, State and Region types. Why?
questions.explain: Each anonymous nested object is a separate type, so the same work was repeated for every one of them. The union of paths is still large either way; naming saves the repeated computation.
options: Named types are erased before checking
The compiler caches a generic type applied to the same named type, so Paths<City> was computed once and reused for every city
Named types have fewer properties
Anonymous types are always any

questions.q: An inferred object type appears several times in a declaration file. What does this count print?
questions.explain: Every place that exports a value with an inferred type repeats the whole structure. A named interface writes it once, and dependents compare a cached named type instead of a fresh structural one.
options: 3 1 true
1 1 false
3 3 true
3 1 false

questions.q: What does isolatedDeclarations make possible for a monorepo build?
questions.explain: The price is writing types for every export whose type would otherwise be inferred. The lesson's catalogue shows where that hurts: Zod schemas are values with inferred types.
options: Running JavaScript without compiling
Producing each file's .d.ts without the type checker, so dependent projects can start as soon as declarations exist instead of waiting for full checks
Skipping declaration files entirely
Sharing one .tsbuildinfo between projects

questions.q: What does the .tsbuildinfo file of an incremental build store?
questions.explain: With it, the lesson's second run with nothing changed dropped from 3,779 types to 340 and from 3,954 instantiations to 0.
options: A copy of node_modules
Fingerprints of the files, the errors found in each, and the shape of each file's declarations, so the next run can re-check only what changed
The compiled JavaScript
A list of the project's npm scripts

questions.q: In the lesson's Vitest project, an incremental run with no changes did almost no checking, but the total time barely changed. Why?
questions.explain: Incremental builds skip checking, not reading. They pay off in large, type-heavy projects, where checking dominates.
options: Incremental builds do not work with Vitest
All 297 files were still read and parsed; in that small project parsing, not checking, took most of the time
The .tsbuildinfo file was deleted
The measurement was wrong

questions.q: A package has "incremental": true and "outDir": "dist", and nothing else about build info. After rm -rf dist && tsc, the build exits with 0. What is in dist?
questions.explain: This is the trap ZudoJS hit in four packages. Setting "tsBuildInfoFile": "./dist/.tsbuildinfo" makes the clean step delete the build information too.
options: The freshly compiled files
Nothing: the .tsbuildinfo next to tsconfig.json survived and says everything is up to date, so no files are written
Only the declaration files
An error log

questions.q: A repository check looks for packages whose build information would survive rm -rf dist. What does it print?
questions.explain: Without tsBuildInfoFile, the file goes next to tsconfig.json. A cache folder in node_modules survives too. Only files inside the folder the clean step deletes are safe.
options:
@shop/http: build info at tsconfig.tsbuildinfo survives a clean of dist/
@shop/auth: build info at node_modules/.cache/auth.tsbuildinfo survives a clean of dist/
@shop/http: build info at tsconfig.tsbuildinfo survives a clean of dist/

@shop/auth: build info at node_modules/.cache/auth.tsbuildinfo survives a clean of dist/
@shop/logger: build info at lib/.tsbuildinfo survives a clean of lib/
Nothing: all four are safe

questions.q: What does an exit code of 0 from tsc prove?
questions.explain: After a build, check that the expected outputs exist, especially before publishing. The lesson's exercise writes such a check.
options: That every output file was written
Only that no errors were found; it does not prove that anything was emitted
That the project is up to date and published
That tests passed

questions.q: How do project references reduce the work of type checking a large repository?
questions.explain: One huge program becomes many small ones. tsc -b --builders sets how many independent projects TypeScript 7 builds at once.
options: They switch off checking for referenced projects
Each project checks only its own files against its dependencies' .d.ts output, unchanged declarations stop rebuilds from rippling, and independent projects can build in parallel
They merge all projects into one program
They cache results on a server

questions.q: The counts say a change made checking expensive, but not where. What does --generateTrace give you?
questions.explain: Look for the widest spans first. There is one types file per checker because TypeScript 7 checks in parallel.
options: A list of slow npm packages
An event timeline (trace.json) to open in a trace viewer, showing which files and expressions the checker spent time on, plus files listing the types each checker created
A fixed version of the slow type
A CPU profile of your application

questions.q: Why does the lesson's CI budget check compare a count (types or instantiations) rather than check time?
questions.explain: A reliable budget turns "the build feels slower" into a specific failing check on the pull request that caused it.
options: Check time is not printed by tsc
Times vary with the machine and its load, so a time budget fails at random or is too loose to catch anything; counts only change when the code or compiler does
Counts are always smaller numbers
Budgets must be integers

questions.q: A pull request legitimately needs a bigger union and fails the type-cost budget. What should happen?
questions.explain: The point of a budget is not to forbid growth, but to make sure someone decides on it instead of nobody noticing.
options: Delete the budget check
Raise the budget in the same pull request, so the increase is a visible, reviewed decision
Retry CI until it passes
Move the type into a .d.ts file

questions.q: Order references look like ORD- plus five digits. What does the lesson recommend instead of a template literal union of all of them?
questions.explain: A brand costs the compiler nothing and still stops plain strings from being passed where a checked reference is required. The format check happens once, at runtime, where the data arrives.
options: A union of the first 1,000 references
A branded string type created only by a function that checks the format at runtime
any
A numeric enum

questions.q: A CI script extracts counts from --extendedDiagnostics output. What does it print?
questions.explain: The filter drops lines whose value ends in s (times), keeping only the stable counts. Object.fromEntries turns the name and number pairs into an object.
options: { Files: 600, Lines: 127223, Types: 16468, Instantiations: 100388 }
{ Files: 600, Lines: 127223, Types: 16468, Instantiations: 100388, 'Check time': 0.278 }

questions.q: These are the real instantiation counts of the full Paths type at depths 3 to 6 (six keys per level). What does this print?
questions.explain: Each level multiplies the work by close to the number of keys per level. A factor that stays roughly constant from level to level is the signature of exponential growth.

questions.q: A runtime analogy for why naming repeated shapes helps: the same work, with and without a cache. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both give the same answer, but the cached version computes each distinct shape once. The compiler does the same for a generic type applied to the same named type, which is why naming City, State and Region cut the instantiations so sharply. Anonymous nested objects are all different shapes, so nothing can be reused.

questions.q: A runtime analogy for tail position: recursion that nests versus work done in a loop. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each nested call waits for the next, so a million of them overflow the call stack. The loop carries its result along and never nests. Tail-recursive conditional types let the compiler work like the loop, which is why they are allowed far more iterations.
options:
RangeError
1000000

RangeError
RangeError

TypeError
1000000

questions.q: Write readCounts(output) that returns the Files, Types and Instantiations numbers from --extendedDiagnostics output, and compare(before, after) that prints each count's growth as a percentage (rounded), in the form Types: +12%.
questions.explain: Comparing counts turns a vague "it feels slower" into a number a reviewer can discuss. Here a change added no files but half again as many instantiations, which points at a new generic or recursive type.

questions.q: Write the runtime version of the lesson's capped Paths type: listPaths(settings, maxDepth) returns every dotted path through a nested object, but no deeper than maxDepth segments.
questions.explain: The depth counter plays the role of the tuple in the type version: every level uses one, and at zero the recursion stops. Counting the output of a function like this is a quick way to estimate how big the type version's union would be.

questions.q: Write templateSize(parts) for a template literal type made of several unions (each given as its list of members): return the number of strings the type would contain, and print whether it is under 100,000 members.
questions.explain: A template literal type is the cross product of its parts, so sizes multiply. A fixed part (like "ORD-" or ":") counts as one; every union multiplies the total.

questions.q: Write checkBudgets(results, budgets): for each measured file, print OK or OVER with the file name, the metric and the budget, and return the number of files over budget. Files without a budget are reported as NO BUDGET (and count as a failure).
questions.explain: Unbudgeted files fail on purpose: a new expensive type should arrive with a stated budget. The return value becomes the script's exit code in CI.
questions.expected:
OVER paths-full.ts: 6100 types, budget 3000
OK paths-capped.ts: 870 types, budget 3000
NO BUDGET routes.ts (1200 types)
failures: 2

questions.q: Write missingOutputs(expected, written) that returns the expected output files that are not in the list of files a build wrote, and print a failure line when any are missing. (In a real script, written would come from listing dist.)
questions.explain: The stale-build-info trap produces an empty dist and exit code 0. Checking for the files that exports promises catches it before anything is published.

questions.q: Complete the capped Paths type so that it stops after two segments, and print a valid path. (The line with @ts-expect-error must stay an error, which proves the cap works.)
questions.explain: The counter tuple grows by one element per level; when its length reaches the cap, the type returns never, and `${K}.${never}` contributes nothing. The @ts-expect-error line is a type test that the cap really applies.
